chapter_theme: Civakan finishes training the king's sons in arms; the delighted king, after a mock threat to fetter him, gives him his daughter Kanakamalai as a bride already fated to an archer, and the two are wed and enjoy each other; the narrator then turns to Rajamapuram, where Civakan's brother, searching for him, comes to Gandharvadattai as she sings three stanzas of a deserted woman's lament.

cast.role: the hero, teacher of arms to the king's sons and husband of Kanakamalai
the king of the city where Civakan teaches, father of Kanakamalai and the princes (called காவலன், மன்னன், வேந்தன் here; the name is traditional and not in these verses)
the king's sons, Civakan's pupils in arms (குமரர், மைந்தர்)
the king's daughter, whom Civakan marries (பாவை, நங்கை, கோதை here; the name is the ilampakam's title)
the people of the city who watch and misread the king's words
Civakan's Vidyadhara wife in Rajamapuram, who sings of separation
Gandharvadattai's companion, addressed in her songs

1677.reading: The spear-handed princes, riding elephants, take from their keen teacher, exactly as the treatise lays it down, how to hide between the elephant's legs, wheel at its trunk, roll at its tail and plunge between its tusks.
1677.nuance: நூலிடைக் கிடந்தவாறே, 'just as it lies in the book', makes the elephant craft a written science that Civakan transmits faithfully rather than a skill he invents.
1677.event: Civakan teaches the king's sons the moves of fighting on and around the war elephant.

1678.reading: Learning without concealment the fighting of the tall-bannered chariot, of the elephant and of the fast horse, and knowing where each fits the sword, the great bow and the lance, they become warriors whose quality even the gods could hardly describe.
1678.nuance: கரப்பற, 'with nothing held back', credits the teacher as much as the pupils: he kept no secret of his art from them.
1678.event: The princes complete their training in chariot, elephant and horse combat and in sword, bow and lance.

1679.reading: Reporting that the princes, proud in fierce war, can break an army, and do not flag in victory even when kings bear down on their force while they stand alone apart from their own lines, they bring them to the king ringed by his army, and he says 'bring them in'.
1679.nuance: Who brings them is not named (உய்த்தார்); line 1, தனியிடம் ஒற்றி, may mean fighting alone apart from the army or something else, and the reading is offered tentatively.
1679.event: The princes are presented to their father the king, who orders them brought before him.

1680.reading: Clearing from the bow the dust that gathers like a cloud, drawing the fine bow's arrow until it touches the earring at the brow, splitting a thread with a shot in the blink of an eye, the eager princes enter the arena and amaze all with their wheeling movements, darting like lightning.
1680.nuance: Line 1 (மழையொடு சூழ்ந்து கொண்ட வான்துகள் சிலையின் நீக்கி) is hard to construe: it may be clearing dust or scattering a cloud of arrows; சாரியை names the formal circling movements of combat display.
1680.event: The princes display their archery and their circling manoeuvres before the king.

1681.reading: Everyone praises them: in archery this one is Vijaya himself, in the lance another is Murugan, another in the sword bends all directions, one firm in elephant and chariot fighting is Achala of unmoving fame, and another without blemish is master of the horse.
1681.nuance: The verse seems to name the princes (விசயன், perhaps அதம்பன் or கதம்பன், அசலன்) each with the arm he excels in, but the run-together script makes several names and their divisions uncertain; the comparisons to Vijaya (Arjuna) and Murugan are the clear part.

1682.reading: Seeing his sons' accomplishment the king gazes with cooled eyes and says that such excellence comes from no one but a king or one twice-born; he will put the youth in fetters and keep him under guard: bring the young bull at once.
1682.nuance: The 'fetter' (நிகளம்) is a joke whose point 1684 reveals: he means to bind Civakan by marriage. His inference from skill to birth happens to be true, since Civakan is a king's son unknown to him, so the story neither confirms nor answers the claim as a rule.
1682.event: The delighted king orders Civakan brought, saying he will fetter him and keep him.

claims.claim: such mastery in teaching arms belongs only to one born a king or a twice-born

1683.reading: Not grasping what the king meant, the crowd thinks that learning too seems a cruel thing, since the king now cruelly imprisons the youth, and stands pitying him while the prince himself loses heart; the king takes the bowman aside and says this.
1683.nuance: The crowd's maxim, கல்வியும் கொடிது போலும், is answered at once: 1684 shows the 'imprisonment' to be a reward, so the reflection stands as a misreading of the king's குறிப்பு. பாபிந்து in line 3 is read as பரிந்து.
1683.event: The people and Civakan take the king's words for a real arrest, and the king draws Civakan aside to speak.

claims.claim: learning can turn against the one who has it, bringing him to harm

1684.reading: The king tells the prince, like a fighting tusker whose tusks are wholly bowed in wounds, that he has put into his hands not the earth alone but heaven too; he feels he has eyes all over his body, sees no way to repay the young bull, and says the girl whose sweet words outdo all music is his.
1684.nuance: The 'fetter' of 1682 turns out to be the bride: the joke depends on the king's word நிகளம் and the crowd's mistaking it. கண்முழுது உடம்பிற் பெற்றேன், 'I have got eyes over my whole body', says his joy needs more eyes to see his sons.
1684.event: The king offers his daughter to Civakan in return for training his sons.

claims.claim: a service that wins one earth and heaven has no repayment that can match it

1685.reading: When the crowned king had spoken, the prince of the clustered spear, his mind of one shape and his word of another, declined; then the king, whose spear gleams having tasted flesh, took his forearm in his own hand and spoke with words like a thundering drum.
1685.nuance: தேற்றான் at line 1 and the phrase மனனொன்றாக வாக்கொன்றா மறுத்தல் are read as the custom of a first refusal: his heart consents while his words decline. If தேற்றான் means 'reassured', the sense changes.
1685.event: Civakan politely declines in words though willing at heart, and the king grasps his arm and presses the offer.

1686.reading: The king says that when the maiden like the golden lady of the lotus, with kaavi-flower eyes, was born, the wise gathered and cast her horoscope by rule without straying from the three, and declared her the due of the one whose bow speeds arrows; and Civakan consents.
1686.nuance: The bride is promised not as a reward alone but as fated: the reckoning made her உரியள், 'rightfully belonging', to a master of the bow, and Civakan's archery training is the sign that fulfils it. மூவியல் is unclear (perhaps three factors of the reckoning).
1686.event: The king cites the birth horoscope that destined his daughter for an archer, and Civakan agrees to the marriage.

claims.claim: a horoscope cast by rule at birth fixes the man a girl belongs to

1687.reading: They dress the girl with the bodice-bound breasts and the long-armed archer in festive finery, announce the good wedding day, and with the whole world knowing, drums sounding, he weds her by the fire and drinks the young delight of the garlanded one.
1687.nuance: பாரெலாம் அறிய, 'with all the earth knowing', and the fire (தீவேட்டு) mark this as an open wedding, in contrast to the secret unions of some earlier ilampakams.
1687.event: Civakan marries Kanakamalai by the fire rite, publicly, and they are united.

1688.reading: Her breasts, like young swelling coconuts, become a musth elephant: the pearls are its forehead plate, it throws off the goad called shame, strips the face-cloth called sandal paste, drives the fierce fight to rout and tramples the fresh garland in its joy.
1688.nuance: நாணெனுந் தோட்டி, 'the goad called shame', makes நாண் the control the elephant shakes off: in love her modesty is dropped, not lost.
1688.event: The couple's lovemaking is told as the charge of an elephant.

1689.reading: With jewelled earrings swinging, golden ear-rolls flashing, girdles jingling, anklets ringing and pearls, wreath and gold chain beating on her bright breasts, the woman sports with the lovely prince.

1690.reading: After the bee-thronged ford of her hips, the elephant is captured: tied to the flawless posts of her breasts with the jewel-chain of her soft arms, goaded by the faultless diamond of her sword-eyes, the forehead ornament on her brow, and fed her nectared red mouth as its flawless mouthful.
1690.nuance: The elephant figure of 1688 is turned round: there her breasts were the rampant elephant; here he is the elephant she captures and tames.
1690.event: The lovemaking is told as the capture and taming of an elephant.

1691.reading: Sinking into the broad hill of the peerless one's chest, her red casket-like breasts reddening as they press, she looks like the desire-vine that clings to the wishing tree and never lets go, giving forth the riches of love.
1691.nuance: கற்பக மரம் and காம வல்லி are the wish-granting tree and its creeper of the celestial world; the image makes the union a heavenly enjoyment, the fruit of merit.

1692.reading: Burning with desire, never letting him go by night or day, the one with shoulders that shame the bamboo, whose speech beguiles the young parrot, drinks without taking her mouth away the beauty of the one who surpasses Murugan, as if it were the nectar of the great sea.
1692.event: Kanakamalai delights in Civakan night and day.

1693.reading: They say that the beloved of the king whose army is like the shore-bound sea, the mountain-chested one, stayed there day after day enjoying the bright beauty of the garlanded woman, of whom it is said the sea's nectar had taken life.
1693.nuance: என்ப, 'they say', puts the narrator at a distance from the scene just as he turns away from it.
1693.event: Civakan stays on in the king's city with his bride.

1694.reading: While the young bull lives on, lying among the swelling breasts of the sword-eyed one, clasping her with his arms and drinking the nectar of her coral mouth, I begin to tell what befell, in Kattiyankaran's old city, those who were close to the hero of the fierce spear.
1694.nuance: The narrator's own first person (விளம்பல் உற்றேன்) marks the change of scene from Civakan's pleasures to the people he left behind in Rajamapuram.

1695.reading: The hero's younger brother, desolate as the stars that have lost the white moon, unable to learn where the wise, counsel-rich one was, searched the good land of dripping honey with a grieving mind and came to the bright city.
1695.nuance: Line 3 (புண்மதித்து உடைந்த போது) is obscure, and which city ஒளிநகர் means is not said here; the image of stars without the moon is the patikam's own (verse 23).
1695.event: Nandattan, failing to find his brother, searches the land and comes to the city.

1696.reading: As the strong one goes to ask the only daughter of the king of the silver mountain, the spear-eyed doll in bright jewels, the woman with the thick-petalled garland takes her well-made vina to play a tune of her own setting.
1696.nuance: Gandharvadattai is a Vidyadhara princess with arts beyond the human, which is why the brother comes to her; the song she sets herself (தானே இட்டதோர் வண்ணம்) comes first.
1696.event: Nandattan goes to Gandharvadattai to ask after Civakan, and she takes up her vina.

1697.reading: Fixing the strings of red gold, firm as if poured from molten ghee, tightening the pegs to their full measure until the joined fingers of her bangled hand redden, the woman with the opening garland sings the song with resolve.
1697.nuance: மாத்திரை names the measured pitch to which the strings are tightened, the technical vocabulary of the vina the poem has used since the vina contest.
1697.event: Gandharvadattai tunes her vina and begins to sing.

1698.reading: He who feared my slender waist would snap if I wore a flower, and scattered the fragrant flowers from his hand, does not come near; he has left me; as he leaves, my bangles leave my shoulders too and my eyes rain pearls without rest: friend, am I to pass away?
1698.nuance: The verb துற runs through the stanza: the lover துறந்தார், and so the bangles துறப்ப; his old tenderness, fearing a flower too heavy for her, is set against his leaving. The plural forms (நண்ணார், துறந்தார்) are honorific.

1699.reading: He who thought my fine waist could not bear the weight of a flower garland and would not hold, does not think of me; he has left me; as he leaves, my bangles leave my shoulders and my spear-eyes cannot sleep: friend, am I to be bewildered?
1699.nuance: The second stanza of the set repeats the first's frame, changing the verb of his neglect (எண்ணார்) and of her suffering (மருள்வேனோ).

1700.reading: He who, saying my waist ached when the bees buzzed, would wave the flower garland to drive them off, does not join me; he has left me; as he leaves, my rounded bangles leave my shoulders and my flower-eyes cannot sleep: friend, am I to grieve?
1700.nuance: The third stanza closes the set: his care went as far as fanning bees from her waist, which makes the absence the sharper. The three stanzas move from death (கழிவேனோ) to bewilderment to grief.

links.note: The king says such excellence belongs only to a king or a twice-born; the couplet says the learned low-born outrank the unlearned high-born.
links.teaches: Read together they show the epic using learning as a sign that betrays hidden royal birth, the reverse of the Kural's use of learning to override birth rank; the conflict holds on reading the king's line as a general rule rather than a compliment.

gains.a: The king's remark is exposed as a claim about birth that the Kural explicitly denies, not just praise of a teacher.
gains.b: The couplet meets a narrative where its opponent's view is spoken by a sympathetic king and even happens to be right about the man in question.

links.note: Both speak of a help weighed against earth and heaven: the couplet says they cannot repay it; the king says the help itself gave him earth and heaven, and finds no requital.
links.teaches: The pair shows a king accepting the couplet's verdict that such a debt is unpayable and answering it with a daughter, so the unpayable gift becomes a bond of marriage instead of a repayment.

gains.a: The king's 'I see no requital' is placed within the Kural's doctrine of gratitude, which explains why he does not offer wealth.
gains.b: The couplet's abstract measure of earth and heaven gets a case where the debtor still acts, choosing kinship over payment.

links.note: Both have the bangles slip as the sign of the man's leaving, and both use the verb துற for his going.
links.teaches: Where the Kural's bangles announce that he has left, the epic's refrain makes the bangles leave as he left, so the body imitates the desertion it reports.

gains.a: The epic princess's song is placed in the Kural's grammar of separation, showing the convention it is varying.
gains.b: The couplet's single image is unfolded into a three-stanza refrain that links his former tenderness to the bangles' going.

links.note: The crowd grieves at the binding of Civakan in Rajamapuram and again at the king's threat of fetters here.
links.teaches: The poet replays Civakan's arrest as comedy: the crowd that once wept for real bonds now weeps for a fetter that proves to be a bride, so the second scene answers the first.

links.note: Kemasari's birth reckoning names her husband by a sign; Kanakamalai's names him as a master of the bow.
links.teaches: Held together they show the Cintamani's pattern of licensing each marriage by a birth horoscope, so the hero's many brides are presented as fate fulfilled rather than conquest.

links.note: Gandharvadattai's horoscope placed her destined husband in Rajamapuram; Kanakamalai's names him by his bow.
links.teaches: The first bride's horoscope and this one frame the series: from the first marriage the stars, not the hero's pursuit, name his wives, and here Civakan's teaching of arms itself becomes the sign.

links.note: The patikam foretold that the younger brother, like a star that lost the moon, would come at a woman's bidding; here the image returns and Gandharvadattai appears.
links.teaches: The pairing identifies the patikam's unnamed woman as Gandharvadattai, whose song follows, and shows the brother's search starting exactly as the patikam framed it.

new_concepts.gloss: music: the lute, melody, mode and the sounds compared to them
new_concepts.label_source: label as declared in earlier Cintamani marks; here the vina (வீணை, 1696) and song (கீதம், 1697)

new_concepts.gloss: an omen or sign read as foretelling what will come
new_concepts.label_source: label from 1129; here the birth horoscope cast by rule (சாதக முறையிற் செய்தார், 1686)

source_issues: 1683 line 3: பாபிந்து is not a word; read as பரிந்து (pitying).
1699 line 4: மணணார்வேற் looks like a misprint for மண்ணார்வேற்.
1699 line 3 has இனவளையும் where the parallel stanzas have நனிவளையும் and கோல்வளையும்; possibly a misprint.
1681: the princes' names run together and cannot be divided with confidence.
Many verses carry the flag 'stanza printed in 8 half-lines; joined into 4 lines'; the joins read correctly.
